newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Saddam has little Iraqi power to back up words.
newsitem.headline: Saddam has little Iraqi power to back up words.

text.p: After six years of confrontation with the United States, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein has the same unyielding language but even less military power to back it up.

Saddam's words following the U.S. missile attack on Tuesday were as uncompromising as ever, rejecting a Western ban on where his airforce can fly and calling on his troops to enter into an unequal struggle with the American war machine.

"You men of our air defence, consider their damned imaginary lines north of the 36th parallel and south of the 32nd parallel non-existent and hit back with capability and efficiency...(at) any hostile plane violating the airspace of your country," Saddam said in a speech carried live on Iraqi media.

Carrying out those orders, directed at both anti-aircraft gunners and pilots, would require an air engagement that Iraq avoided even when it had the far more formidable force that captured Kuwait in 1990.

Western diplomatic sources have long complained of Saddam's efforts to rebuild the forces demolished by the U.S.-led coalition that liberated Kuwait in 1991. They charged that missile parts intercepted in Amman a year ago reflected Saddam's efforts to smuggle military spares that have gone on since his defeat in the Gulf War.

His diminished tank forces can still subdue lightly armed opponents inside the official borders of Iraq, such as the Kurds they drove from the northern city of Arbil last weekend or the Shiites of southern Iraq who were crushed when they rebelled after the Gulf War.

But, despite efforts to circumvent U.N. controls on arms and U.S. warnings of Iraqi military strength, the Iraqi military is not the well-equipped force that battled Iran for eight brutal years in the 1980s or the "million man" arm that was expected to be a formidable adversary in the 1991 Gulf War.

While Western sources say Iraqi aircraft fly more than a 1,000 sorties a month, it is no longer the airforce of 1990. At the outbreak of the Gulf War even those planes were either locked in bunkers or flown to safety in Iran, where they were permanently impounded.

The Republic Guards, Iraq's best fighting force, who were lined up in 1993 in a fresh threat to invade Kuwait, were a ragged-looking force. Some had holes in their boots and those interviewed afterwards expressed immense relief they had not crossed the border.

The only area where Saddam has a stronger hand than in 1991 is on the diplomatic front. Britain is the only country showing wholehearted enthusiasm for the U.S. attacks, while France and Russia -- who both supported the war over Kuwait -- sound unconvinced. That, however, would be unlikely to deter more U.S. military action if Saddam continues the confrontation.

"It will be a glorious day the Iraqi people will write down, in the name of the Almighty, in their chronicle of great honour," Saddam, dressed in a field marshal's uniform, said on Tuesday in a typically unbowed reaction to the U.S. raids.
"For the aggressors it will be a day of cursing in history as well as on the level of the globe following the curse that has befallen them from God."

But Saddam has a long pattern of confrontation with the West punctuated by uncompromising speeches -- including previous rejections of no-fly zones imposed by the West -- followed eventually by an unacknowledged defeat or a quiet climbdown.

Before the fight over Kuwait in 1991, he promised victory in the "mother of all battles." Since his overwhelming defeat, Saddam has delivered annual speeches declaring the military disaster a great victory.
